A man’s door clicked shut behind me, and I was out on the street again in the hour when the sky slowly launders the blue out of the day. Early autumn, or late summer—the kind of evening that behaves like ice cream left out, softening so quietly you don’t notice until it has pooled at your feet in violet. I hadn’t planned to walk. The bus stop was forty yards away, and the next bus was either arriving or had just gone, and I discovered I no longer cared which, so I turned left instead of right and walked toward the tall buildings, the density of them, the rim of the world where the city gives itself to the river.

There is no such thing as walking aimlessly. Every step is a decision, even if the decision is merely to continue. Within a few blocks I became aware that my body had taken the route it always takes when it doesn’t want to go home—not a shortcut but a sort of pilgrimage along the backs of buildings, where the light is older and the walls have seen too much wallpaper. The pavement was still warm; the air had in it the exhaust of buses, and farther off fried onions, cut grass, somebody’s laundry: the city’s evening casserole. A man in a gray tracksuit was watering the little strip of plants outside his restaurant, watering them even though it had just rained. I think he was not watering the plants but watering the evening, holding the hiss of water up against the silence of the street.

I passed a barbershop whose sign buzzed even in autumn, a fluorescent whale in the twilight. Inside, a man was getting his hair cut. The barber circled him like a planet around a sun, humming, snipping; the customer sat as still as people ever sit except when being prayed over or asleep. There is a profound trust in letting someone stand that close to your ears with scissors. We surrender our heads to strangers the way we surrender our minds to sleep, and I have always found the ordinary heroism of that gesture a little moving. He would go home lighter, changed by a pound of hair, and no one would tell him he looked different in quite the right way. I wondered if he would ever know that an unknown person stood in the street and looked at his reflected stillness and felt briefly tender about the whole human species. Probably not. That is the economy of noticing: you pay with attention, and the account goes to no one.

Further on, past a parking garage and a derelict dry cleaner’s, a bakery was closing for the night. The woman at the counter was pulling down a metal shutter, and the warm yeasty ghost of the day’s bread came out to embrace the sidewalk once, twice, like a patient saying goodbye at the door. I stopped and breathed. Bread is the best argument civilization has ever produced: flour, water, salt, time, and fire, with a margin for error wide enough for the whole human race. It is also one of the only things that makes you slow down, because you have to knead and wait and knead and wait, and then there is that moment when you pull it from the oven and the whole apartment turns into a temple. Bakeries have understood for ten thousand years that the scent of bread is a kind of law, and that people will follow it anywhere.

I walked on. A slender crate of secondhand paperbacks sat on the curb outside a used-book shop that had also closed; the owner had forgotten to take them in. Many spines were bleached by many summers, titles promising things that had been kept elsewhere. I picked up a thin volume of poems and opened it at random. On the title page someone had written a name, a year, and nothing else. I wondered whether the inscription had been a gift, or a claim of ownership, and whether the book had been loved, and where the hand that wrote it was now. Sometimes a book finds you in a gutter begging to be rescued. But I had nowhere to put it. I laid it back in the crate like a sleeping animal and asked its forgiveness. There is a joy in touching paper books that is hard to describe to people who have only read screens. They are solid, heavy with memory; they carry the history of their readers in creases, opinions, coffee rings. Reading is the closest thing to visiting the dead, because you hear voices that have stopped speaking. And sometimes, in the margins, you find the handwriting of someone else—a chair left out for a guest who never returned.

A few doors down, a laundromat glowed like an aquarium. The washing machines were churning their pastel contents; a young man sat on the folding table with his headphones on, staring at the dryer as if it contained his future. There is something hypnotic about the tumble of clothes, the way things are exposed to each other in the whiteness, tumbling and tumbling. People’s shirts slap against other people’s sheets; the world does laundry like a giant mixing the ingredients of a cake. The young man maybe felt lonely, maybe didn’t; the machine was going on his behalf. Machines have a strange gentleness when they imitate the old chores of washing and spinning; they are not cold at all. They are just enormous hands with water inside them.

By the time I reached the square, the sky had gone from indigo to the deep navy of a Christmas card, and in the center of the plaza a wedding party had gathered under strings of bulbs. They were laughing; they were too loud for twenty feet away but nobody minded. The bride held her bouquet behind her back like a secret she hadn’t decided to share. I felt a flicker of joy for them, then a tuft of melancholy—the strange capacity of the heart to be happy for others and sad for itself at the same time, two channels on the same mixing board. A man in a waistcoat was nibbling the ears of a toddler seated on his shoulder, and the toddler was laughing with the pure abandon of a teakettle. That is the thing about weddings: they ring with the high notes of all our little dreams, even the ones that have gone flat elsewhere. It is not that we believe nothing will go wrong; it is that in that hour we can hear the whole orchestra tuning.

And then the rain arrived without asking, as it does. It pattered on the awning of a pharmacy where I took cover, the sound of a hundred fingers drumming on a tabletop, impatient but not unkind. Beside me stood a woman with a string bag full of vegetables. She moved the bag closer to her feet. Neither of us spoke. There is a peculiar intimacy in sharing a roof with a stranger: you share air, you listen to the same water, and you silently promise that when the rain ends you will part and remember each other only as a sleeve and a shadow. I found it restful. Hospitals have waiting rooms; airports have gates; life has these small covered intervals, and we rarely give them credit. I could smell the cilantro in her string bag; she could probably smell my wet coat. We were an encyclopedia of each other’s lives, published in an edition of one, never printed again.

When the rain eased, I continued, passing a cinema. Half the letters on the old marquee had burned out, so the title read as an abbreviation, a haiku of lost vowels. Inside, someone was projecting a movie I would never see onto a screen I couldn’t see, and I could imagine the auditorium: its warmth, its darkness, the collective breathing of strangers who had paid to sit in the dark and be moved, or at least distracted. We are the only animals that make up stories and pay to be scared by them. I think that is bizarre and magnificent and worth remembering when we grow too serious about the usefulness of art.

On a side street a small playground stood silent under a wet slide, a swing moving in the wind as if pushed by an invisible child. For a moment the world felt full of ghosts—not scary ones, just the weight of everyone who had ever played there: their shouts, scuffed knees, parents on benches checking watches, the faint sour smell of sun on plastic. Time is generous in its way; it lets us visit again the places we used to be, or the places we used to be in other people’s lives. I stood there longer than I meant to. A cat sat on the stoop of a corner house, watching me watch the playground, and its face said, in the only language cats can say, *nothing here is yours, and yet it is.*

I passed a mural covering the entire side of a building: enormous faces, children with flowers in their mouths, a fox, a gear train, a line of hands raised like a fence. Public art is a city’s dream diary, and this one was especially dreamed. I wondered who had painted it, on what borrowed scaffolds, in what season. The paint was already fading, the yellow going pale as straw, but it still did its job: it broke the monotony of the block, a hole in the world in the best sense. People think artists are doing something decorative. Actually they are punching holes in the walls of the ordinary so that the light gets in.

My phone buzzed in my pocket. I took it out to check the time, then found myself scrolling to the name of someone I hadn’t called in months. I opened the messaging window, staring at the blank input bar. There are conversations you rehearse for years and never deliver; they live inside you finished and unfinishable. The cursor blinked at me like an eye. I put the phone away. Some thoughts are meant for rivers, not for telegraphs. I have noticed that the more urgent a message seems, the more likely it was always a letter to yourself.

I kept walking. The neighborhood loosened, the buildings lowered themselves, the street widened, and then the river held the sky. At the bridge I leaned on the railing and looked down at the water. The city hummed behind me, but the sound went thin and wavery, as if the water had turned down the volume. Lamps along the promenade had come on, each one a small lighthouse for the drowned shimmer floating on the surface. And of course I thought of all the steps that had brought me here—not mine only, but the city’s, the bridge’s, and that strange compounding of choices that makes the future sprout from the present like branches from a trunk that looks arbitrary from any one vantage point. We think of our lives as arrows, but they are sprawling rhizomes; every step digs a sideways root. A couple walked past me eating fried squid from a paper cone; the woman laughed at something the man said, and the laugh went across the water and echoed off the underside of the bridge. They will not remember me. I will not remember them, except in this sentence.

A car stopped at the traffic light, and from its open window came a snatch of a song I hadn’t heard in years, some old love song, and for a second I was somewhere else, another season, another river. That is how memory works: a song, a smell, a certain angle of light, and the past tips forward into the present like a glass of water that knocks over and spreads across the whole table. You never step into the same river twice, but you also never hear the same song once; it is always the river and the ghost of the river.

I stayed at the railing until I was cold. Then I retraced, not my steps exactly, but a parallel route, one street in, so the walk back was a different walk, a commentary on the first, like looking at the same sand dune from the other side. I passed the same barbershop, now dark, the chairs like small thrones waiting for the morning. I passed the pharmacy, the awning still running with water. I passed the laundromat, where the young man was folding his clothes with a new decency, holding each shirt up before folding it, as if to say goodbye. I passed a construction site where a crane stood skeletal against the sky, a prehistoric animal frozen mid-stride. For a moment I recognized the city as a living system of lights and hungers, all of it slowly building and unbuilding itself, like a reef made of brick and glass and longing.

My own building stood at the end of a line of identical buildings, and my own door was unremarkable, brown, its paint chipped at the handle where many mornings had fumbled for the lock. I stood there with the key between my fingers and noticed for the first time that the scratches formed a pattern like a fan, a little compass rose of repeated entrances. A hundred thousand nights had blurred into this scratched geometry. I turned the key and stepped inside. The hallway smelled like everyone’s soup and nobody’s.

I made tea. I sat by the window. Somewhere out in the dark, the woman with the string bag was putting away vegetables; the bride was taking off her shoes; the barber was sweeping hair into a dustpan; the bakery was cool and scrubbed; the paperbacks were dreaming in their crate; the river was still carrying the city’s lights south, one by one, like a careful waiter carrying trays of small candles. The rain had gone and left the streets glossy, like a seal that had been pressed wet onto a sleeping envelope. And I understood, gently, that a life isn’t a story but a set of departures and returns, each one a stitch in a garment we can never see whole, though we wear it every day. Tomorrow I would walk out again, through the same scratched door, into the same rearranged world. The street would be the same. The light would be different. It always is. That is the whole trick, and it is also the whole grace.
